text: When the acrylate is a short straight-chain alkyl ester (e.g., OCCCC), its synergy with the epoxide component is highly dependent on epoxide chain length. If the epoxide chain is either too short (≤3 carbons) or too long (≥13 carbons) paired with a short-chain epoxide (≤5 carbons), even at a suitable ratio (e.g., 0.25-0.5), it may still tend toward low transfection efficiency.

When the alkyl chain following the acrylate ester group exceeds 8 carbons, a higher ratio (e.g., ≥0.5) generally tends toward low transfection efficiency; however, at a lower ratio (e.g., ≤0.25) with a branched or optimized ester structure, high transfection efficiency can still occur.

When the epoxide has a long alkyl chain (≥11 carbons, ordinary alkyl), pairing with a short straight-chain acrylate (e.g., OCCCC, 4 carbons) at a low ratio (e.g., ≤0.25) tends toward high transfection efficiency. However, if the acrylate is a medium-to-long straight-chain ester (8-16 carbons) or a branched ester, even at a low ratio (0.25), it tends toward low efficiency. This rule does not apply to fluorinated epoxides or to extremely long-chain epoxides (≥13 carbons) paired with branched acrylates.

When the acrylate is a long straight-chain alkyl ester (≥12 carbons after the ester group) or an unsaturated straight-chain ester, a higher ratio (e.g., ≥0.5) tends toward low transfection efficiency; but at a lower ratio (e.g., ≤0.25) with other components (e.g., epoxide) optimized, high efficiency can still occur. For unsaturated short-chain esters (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC), high efficiency is also possible at a medium ratio (e.g., 0.5) combined with a specific epoxide.
When the acrylate ratio is high (e.g., ≥0.5), it tends toward low transfection efficiency, unless the epoxide has a special structure (e.g., fluorinated) or the ratio combination is atypical.

When the acrylate contains an unsaturated bond (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) at a low ratio (≤0.25), together with a short-chain epoxide (≤4 carbons), high transfection efficiency tends to occur. However, this effect may be strongly influenced by the dioxaphospholane component's structure and may fail when the dioxaphospholane also contains an unsaturated long chain.

When the epoxide contains a perfluoroalkyl chain, its pathways to high transfection efficiency are more diverse. Besides a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC) being effective at a low ratio (0.25), an unsaturated straight-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) can also achieve high efficiency at a low ratio (0.25). The conditions for high efficiency are highly sensitive to the ester component's structure (unsaturation, chain length) and ratio, and the equivalents-to-backbone requirement may be more relaxed than previously understood.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥11 carbons, e.g., CCCCCCCCCCCCC1OC1), even at a low acrylate ratio (e.g., 0.25) with a branched ester (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC), it still tends toward low transfection efficiency. This differs from the phenomenon in which short straight-chain esters (e.g., OCCCC) achieve high efficiency at a low ratio.

When all components (epoxide, dioxaphospholane, acrylate) are present and all at high ratios (e.g., total ratio >1), it tends toward low transfection efficiency, suggesting that an excessively high overall concentration or overly complex formulation may be unfavorable for transfection.

When the epoxide has a relatively short chain (e.g., 5 carbons, CCCCC1OC1), if the acrylate is a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(CC)CCCCC) at a high ratio (e.g., 0.5), high transfection efficiency can still be achieved. This indicates that when a short-chain epoxide is paired with a high proportion of branched ester, there exists a high-efficiency synergistic pathway distinct from that seen with long straight-chain esters.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., OCC1OC1, CC1OC1, CCC1OC1), its synergy with acrylates is complex. At a medium ratio (e.g., 0.5) or higher ratio (e.g., 0.75), it may combine with medium-to-long branched esters (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC, OC(CCC)CCC) or a specific straight-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC) to achieve high transfection efficiency. However, at a low ratio (e.g., ≤0.25) combined with medium-to-long branched esters (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC), it generally tends toward low efficiency. Its high-efficiency pathway is highly sensitive to ester structure, ratio, and backbone equivalents.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(C(F)(F)F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is paired with a specific dioxaphospholane (e.g., branched ester OC(CC)CCCCC) at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), high transfection efficiency may be achieved. However, if the paired dioxaphospholane has an unsuitable structure (e.g., a short unsaturated chain OC/C=C/C, or a long unsaturated chain OCCC/C=C/CCCCC) or is paired with a specific-chain-length acrylate (e.g., a 14-carbon straight-chain ester), it may become inefficient. This challenges the old notion that fluorinated epoxides invariably lead to low efficiency, though its high-efficiency pathway is sensitive to the dioxaphospholane structure.

When the acrylate contains an unsaturated bond and has a short chain (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC), synergy with a specific-chain-length epoxide (e.g., 4-carbon CCCC1OC1) at a medium (e.g., 0.5) or low (e.g., 0.25) ratio may achieve high transfection efficiency, though this effect is not absolute; at a higher ratio (e.g., 0.75) or with a medium-short-chain epoxide (e.g., 5 carbons), it may fail.

When the acrylate is a branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC) at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), if the epoxide chain is extremely short (e.g., OCC1OC1), it tends toward low transfection efficiency, indicating that the synergistic effect of the branched ester may be constrained by the epoxide's backbone length.

When the dioxaphospholane contains a long straight alkyl chain (e.g., OCCCCCCCCCC) and the acrylate is a short straight-chain alkyl ester (OCCCC) at a medium ratio (0.5), high transfection efficiency may be achieved.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., CCC1OC1, CC1OC1), pathways to high transfection efficiency are diverse: besides pairing with a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC, OC(CCCC)CCCC) at a medium (0.5) or higher (0.75) ratio, combining with a specific branched ester at a low ratio (0.25) may also achieve high efficiency, although with a lower success rate and uncertain efficiency.

When the epoxide is medium-to-long chain (e.g., 7-9 carbons), if the acrylate is a medium-to-long straight-chain alkyl ester (8-16 carbons after the ester group), high transfection efficiency may be achieved at a low backbone equivalent (e.g., 2) and a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.5); this rule is particularly applicable to medium-short-chain epoxides of a specific length (e.g., 7 carbons). However, at a higher backbone equivalent (e.g., 3) or a low ratio, such combinations may still be inefficient. This rule does not apply to the synergy between a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC) and a medium-to-long-chain epoxide at a low ratio.

When the dioxaphospholane has a branched ester structure (e.g., OC(C)CCCC, OC(C)CCCCCC) at a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.5), even in the absence of an epoxide component or with an ordinary-chain epoxide, high transfection efficiency may still be achieved synergistically with a specific acrylate (including branched esters). This indicates that branched ester structures also have the potential to optimize transfection when present in the dioxaphospholane component.

When the acrylate is a specific branched ester, its synergy with the epoxide is highly dependent on fine matching of the branched ester structure, epoxide chain length, ratio, and backbone equivalents. For example, certain branched esters may achieve high efficiency with a short-chain epoxide (e.g., 5 carbons) at a specific ratio (e.g., 0.5); at a lower ratio (e.g., 0.25), high efficiency may be achieved with a long-chain epoxide (e.g., 9 carbons) or a specific fluorinated epoxide, though this effect usually requires a higher backbone equivalent (e.g., 3). With a medium-to-long-chain epoxide (e.g., 7-9 carbons), high efficiency may also be achieved at a moderate ratio (0.5) and a lower backbone equivalent (2). Not all branched esters are efficient under all conditions.

A higher backbone equivalent (e.g., 3) helps improve transfection efficiency, but is not strictly necessary; optimized epoxide and acrylate structures (e.g., branched esters) can achieve high efficiency at a lower backbone equivalent (e.g., 2), especially when the epoxide chain length matches the ester structure.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., CC1OC1), if the acrylate ratio is moderate (e.g., 0.5) or paired with a specific branched or medium-to-long-chain ester, high transfection efficiency may be achieved. This effect is most pronounced at a ratio of 0.5, challenging the previous notion that extremely short-chain epoxides are only efficient with branched esters at a low ratio.

When the epoxide has a medium-short chain (5 carbons, e.g., CCCCC1OC1), its synergy with a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(CCC)CCC) is highly dependent on the backbone equivalent. At a backbone equivalent of 3, high transfection efficiency can be achieved at a lower acrylate ratio (0.25); but at an equivalent of 2, the same structure may fail to achieve high efficiency.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥9 carbons), a short straight-chain acrylate (e.g., OCCCC) generally tends toward low transfection efficiency, but branched or unsaturated esters at a low ratio may achieve high efficiency, possibly with a lower required backbone equivalent (e.g., 2).

When the epoxide component is absent (NAN), high transfection efficiency depends on the structural matching between the dioxaphospholane and the acrylate. Besides dioxaphospholanes with an unsaturated long chain or specific branched esters, a combination of an ordinary long straight-chain alkyl ester dioxaphospholane with a specific branched-ester acrylate at a moderate ratio may also achieve high efficiency.

When the epoxide is absent and the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated long chain and a branched ester structure, the likelihood of achieving high transfection efficiency in synergy with the acrylate depends on the acrylate structure: combination with a specific branched ester may be efficient, but combination with an unsaturated short-chain ester may be inefficient.

When the epoxide component is absent (NAN), the conditions for achieving high transfection efficiency are broader. Besides complex dioxaphospholanes containing an unsaturated long chain or specific branched esters, an ordinary long straight-chain alkyl ester dioxaphospholane (e.g., OCCCCCCCCCC) combined with a branched-ester acrylate at a moderate ratio may also be efficient, though this effect is sensitive to the acrylate structure.

When the acrylate is an unsaturated ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) at a high ratio (e.g., 0.5-0.75), its synergy with the epoxide is highly complex. Pairing with an extremely short-chain epoxide (e.g., CC1OC1) at a specific ratio and equivalent may achieve high transfection efficiency (as shown in a new case), but pairing with a medium-short-chain epoxide (e.g., CCCCC1OC1) tends toward low efficiency (see rule_061). Pairing with a long-chain or fluorinated epoxide generally tends toward low efficiency, though exceptions may exist.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is paired with an unsaturated dioxaphospholane (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) and the acrylate is absent (NAN), at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), it tends toward high transfection efficiency. However, this high-efficiency pathway is sensitive to the specific structure of the dioxaphospholane, and combining with an ordinary long-chain ester dioxaphospholane or a specific acrylate may be inefficient.

When the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated long chain together with a branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC, OC(C)CCCCC), if the acrylate is also present and is a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(CC)CCCCC), it tends toward high transfection efficiency; but if the acrylate is a different branched ester (e.g., OC(CCC)CCC) or the ratio is not appropriate (e.g., only the dioxaphospholane present), it may fail. This rule extends the structural understanding of efficient combinations involving unsaturated dioxaphospholanes.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥11 carbons), the conclusion that an unsaturated acrylate (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) tends toward low transfection efficiency requires strict qualification. This tendency mainly holds at a low acrylate ratio (e.g., 0.25), whereas at a medium ratio (e.g., 0.5), combination with a specific ultra-long-chain epoxide (e.g., 13 carbons) may achieve high transfection efficiency.

When the dioxaphospholane has a specific branched ester structure (e.g., O=P1(OC(C)CCCCC)OCCO1) and the epoxide is absent (NAN), pairing with a specific-structure acrylate (e.g., OCCCCCCCC) at a moderate ratio (0.25:0.5) may achieve high transfection efficiency. However, this high-efficiency pathway requires a fairly specific acrylate structure, and not all branched-ester acrylates (e.g., OC(CC)CCC) can match it.

When the dioxaphospholane contains a specific branched ester structure (e.g., OC(C)CCCCC) and the epoxide is absent (NAN), combination with specific acrylate structures may be efficient or inefficient; efficiency depends on the precise structural match between the dioxaphospholane and the acrylate, and not all branched or unsaturated acrylates can form an efficient combination with it.

When the epoxide component is absent (NAN) and the dioxaphospholane is an unsaturated short-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC, OC/C=C/CCC), combination with a specific acrylate (e.g., branched ester OC(C)CCCCCC) at a low ratio (0.25) may achieve high transfection efficiency. However, if the dioxaphospholane's unsaturated chain is too short (e.g., OC/C=C/C), it tends toward low efficiency.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons), pathways to high transfection efficiency are limited. Although synergy with a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC) at a low ratio is possible, combination with medium-to-long branched esters (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC, OC(CCC)CCC) at a low or medium ratio tends toward low efficiency. In addition, the likelihood of high efficiency with an ordinary short straight-chain ester (OCCCC) at a medium ratio (0.5) is also low.

When a fluorinated epoxide is combined with a specific unsaturated long-chain dioxaphospholane (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC), with the acrylate absent (NAN), at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), high transfection efficiency may be achieved. This further extends the understanding that fluorinated epoxides can be efficient when combined with specific unsaturated ester components, independent of specific branched-ester dioxaphospholanes.

When the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated long chain together with a branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC, OC(C)CCCCC), if the acrylate is also present at a high ratio (e.g., 0.5), even if the acrylate is a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC), it still tends toward high transfection efficiency. This revises the earlier view that such combinations are only effective at a low ratio or with a specific branched ester.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(C(F)(F)F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is paired with a long straight-chain alkyl acrylate (≥12 carbons after the ester group, e.g., OCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC) at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), high transfection efficiency may be achieved, indicating that the high-efficiency pathway of fluorinated epoxides is not limited to specific branched or unsaturated esters.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥9 carbons) and the acrylate is a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(CCC)CCC), high transfection efficiency may be achieved at a low acrylate ratio (e.g., 0.25), and the required backbone equivalent may be lower (e.g., 2) rather than restricted to a high equivalent (e.g., 3).

When the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated short-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) and the epoxide is absent (NAN), pairing with a medium-to-long branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC) at a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.25:0.5) may achieve high transfection efficiency, extending the range of efficient synergy for unsaturated-ester dioxaphospholanes in epoxide-free systems.

When the dioxaphospholane contains a branched ester structure (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCCCC) and the epoxide is absent (NAN), pairing with an ordinary long straight-chain alkyl acrylate (e.g., OCCCCCCCC, 8 carbons) at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25:0.5) tends toward low transfection efficiency, indicating that the efficiency of branched-ester dioxaphospholanes is not universal and requires matching with a specific acrylate structure (e.g., branched or unsaturated ester).

When the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated long chain together with a branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC, OC(C)CCCCC), the likelihood of achieving high transfection efficiency in synergy with the acrylate depends on the acrylate's precise structure and ratio combination. Although synergy with certain branched esters (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC, OC(CC)CCCCC) at a moderate ratio may be efficient, synergy with other branched esters (e.g., OC(CC)CCCCC at a low ratio) may be inefficient. This effect is not absolutely universal.

When a fluorinated epoxide is combined with an unsaturated short-chain-ester dioxaphospholane (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC), with the acrylate absent (NAN), at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), high transfection efficiency may also be achieved. This further extends the high-efficiency pathway of fluorinated epoxides combined with unsaturated-ester dioxaphospholanes.

When a fluorinated epoxide is combined with an unsaturated acrylate (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) or a long straight-chain acrylate (≥12 carbons), its high-efficiency synergistic pathways are diverse, not limited to a low ratio (0.25); high efficiency may also be achieved at a medium ratio (e.g., 0.5) or higher ratio (e.g., 0.75). However, its efficiency is highly sensitive to the acrylate's precise structure, ratio, and backbone equivalent, and not all such combinations tend toward high efficiency.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(C(F)(F)F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is paired with an unsaturated acrylate (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) or a long straight-chain acrylate (≥14 carbons), even at a low ratio (0.25), achieving high transfection efficiency is highly sensitive to the acrylate's precise structure (chain length, position of unsaturation) and backbone equivalent, and not all such combinations tend toward high efficiency. This challenges part of the inferences in rule_033 and rule_007.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥9 carbons), its synergy with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CCC)CCC, OC(C)CCCCCC) is highly dependent on the precise match between epoxide chain length and branched-ester structure, as well as the backbone equivalent. For example, a 9-carbon epoxide with OC(CCC)CCC may be efficient at a low ratio, but with OC(C)CCCCCC under similar conditions may be inefficient. When the chain is too long (≥13 carbons), combination with certain branched esters tends toward low efficiency, especially at a lower backbone equivalent.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., CC1OC1, CCC1OC1) and the acrylate is an unsaturated short-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC), synergy at a low acrylate ratio (0.25) tends toward low transfection efficiency. At a medium acrylate ratio (e.g., 0.5), high transfection efficiency may be achieved, but this effect is influenced by the epoxide's exact chain length (e.g., the 4-carbon CCCC1OC1 is more effective), the ratio, the ester structure (e.g., specific branched esters), and the backbone equivalent, and is not universal.

When the epoxide chain is extremely long (≥13 carbons, e.g., CCCCCCCCCCCCC1OC1), its synergy with branched-ester acrylates is highly sensitive to the specific branched-ester structure. For example, OC(CCC)CCC may be efficient at a low ratio (0.25) and low backbone equivalent (2), whereas OC(C)CCCCCC under similar conditions may be inefficient.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(C(F)(F)F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is combined with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CC)CCC), high transfection efficiency may still be achieved at a low backbone equivalent (e.g., 2) and low ratio (0.25). This indicates that the high-efficiency synergistic pathway of fluorinated epoxides is not limited to specific unsaturated esters, and also applies to certain branched esters, with the backbone equivalent requirement possibly more relaxed than previously understood.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., CC1OC1, OCC1OC1), combination with a medium-to-long branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC, OC(CC)CCCCC) at a low ratio (0.25) may tend toward low transfection efficiency, indicating that the efficiency of such combinations requires a higher ratio (e.g., ≥0.5) or a specific backbone equivalent condition.

When the acrylate is an unsaturated short-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC), its synergy with a short-chain epoxide (e.g., CCCC1OC1, CCC1OC1) at a low ratio (0.25) has a low likelihood of achieving high transfection efficiency, and such combinations tend toward low efficiency. This indicates that the high-efficiency synergy of unsaturated esters may require a more specific epoxide chain length (e.g., 4 carbons), ratio (e.g., ≥0.5), or backbone equivalent condition.

When the dioxaphospholane is an unsaturated long-chain ester (e.g., OCCCCCCCC/C=C/C/C=C/CCCCC) and the epoxide is absent, combination with an ordinary straight-chain alkyl acrylate (e.g., OCCCCCCCC, 8 carbons) at a 0.25:0.5 ratio tends toward low transfection efficiency. This indicates that the efficiency of unsaturated-ester dioxaphospholanes is sensitive to the acrylate structure and requires matching with a specific structure (e.g., branched or unsaturated ester).

When the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated long chain and a branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC, OCCCCCCCC/C=C/C/C=C/CCCCC) and the epoxide is absent, even when paired with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CC)CCCCC) at a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.25:0.5), it may still tend toward low transfection efficiency. This indicates that the high-efficiency synergy requirement for the acrylate's precise structure in such complex dioxaphospholanes may be stricter than previously understood, and not all branched esters can achieve an efficient match with it.

When the epoxide is absent and the dioxaphospholane contains an unsaturated long chain and a branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC), combination with most branched-ester acrylates tends toward low efficiency, but with a key exception: combination with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC, OC(CCCC)CCCC) at a moderate ratio may achieve high efficiency. In addition, even when the dioxaphospholane is a specific short-chain branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCC), combination with a matching branched-ester acrylate may also be efficient. Efficiency is highly dependent on the precise structural match between the dioxaphospholane and the acrylate.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥9 carbons, e.g., CCCCCCC1OC1), combination with an ultra-long straight-chain acrylate (≥16 carbons after the ester group, e.g., OCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC) at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25) may achieve high transfection efficiency. This indicates that the high-efficiency pathway of long-chain epoxides can extend to synergy with ultra-long straight-chain esters, distinct from the pathway involving branched esters.

When a medium-short-chain epoxide (e.g., 5 carbons, CCCCC1OC1) is combined with an unsaturated short-chain-ester acrylate (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) at a high ratio (e.g., 0.75), it tends toward low transfection efficiency. This indicates that the high-efficiency synergy of unsaturated esters depends not only on epoxide chain length but also has strict ratio requirements, and a high ratio may suppress its effectiveness.

When the epoxide chain is long (≥9 carbons) and the acrylate is an ultra-long straight-chain ester (≥14 carbons), high transfection efficiency may be achieved at a low ratio (0.25), but this effect is highly sensitive to the specific chain lengths of the epoxide and ester, and is not universally efficient.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is combined with an ordinary short straight-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC), achieving high transfection efficiency is highly sensitive to the acrylate's precise structure, ratio, and backbone equivalent. At a higher backbone equivalent (e.g., 3) and lower ratio (e.g., 0.25), it may be inefficient, indicating that the high-efficiency pathway is not universal.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., CCC1OC1) and the acrylate is a medium-to-long branched ester (e.g., OC(CCCC)CCCC, OC(C)CCCCCC), combinations at a low ratio (e.g., ≤0.25) generally tend toward low efficiency, though this tendency is not absolute. With a specific branched ester (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC) and a lower backbone equivalent (e.g., 2), high transfection efficiency may be achieved even at a low ratio (0.25) or high ratio (0.75). At a medium ratio (e.g., 0.5-0.75), efficiency is highly sensitive to the backbone equivalent and ester structure.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is combined with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CC)CCC, OC(C)CCCCCC), high transfection efficiency may still be achieved even at a medium ratio (e.g., 0.5) and low backbone equivalent (e.g., 2). This extends rule_033's finding regarding the applicable conditions for efficient synergy of fluorinated epoxides, which is not limited to a low ratio.

When the epoxide is absent (NAN) and the dioxaphospholane is a simple alkoxy ester (e.g., OCCC), combination with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CCC)CCC) at a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.25:0.5) may achieve high transfection efficiency. This indicates that an efficient dioxaphospholane structure does not necessarily need to be complex or unsaturated, and matching with a specific branched-ester acrylate is key.

When a fluorinated epoxide (e.g., FC(C(F)(F)F)(F)C(F)(F)C(F)(F)CC1OC1) is combined with an ultra-long straight-chain acrylate (≥16 carbons after the ester group, e.g., OCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC), high transfection efficiency may be achieved at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25) and high backbone equivalent (e.g., 3). This indicates that the high-efficiency synergistic pathway of fluorinated epoxides can extend to matching with ordinary ultra-long straight-chain esters.

When a medium-to-long-chain epoxide (e.g., 9 carbons, CCCCCCCCC1OC1) is combined with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC), high transfection efficiency may be achieved at a higher acrylate ratio (e.g., 0.5) and a medium backbone equivalent (e.g., 2). This challenges rule_017's view that medium-to-long-chain epoxides combined with medium-to-long straight-chain esters tend toward low efficiency, and reveals a potential high-efficiency pathway for specific branched esters at a higher ratio.

When the epoxide is absent (NAN) and the dioxaphospholane has a specific branched ester structure (e.g., OC(C)CCCCC), combination with another branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC) at a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.25:0.5) may achieve high transfection efficiency. This indicates that matching between specific branched esters has efficient synergistic potential, although this effect is not absolutely universal and requires a high degree of precise matching between the dioxaphospholane and acrylate branch structures.

When the epoxide chain is extremely short (≤3 carbons, e.g., CC1OC1), combination with an ordinary short straight-chain alkyl acrylate (e.g., OCCCC, 4 carbons) at a moderate ratio (e.g., 0.5) can still achieve high transfection efficiency; but at a lower ratio (e.g., 0.25), such combinations tend toward low efficiency.

When the epoxide chain is extremely long (≥13 carbons, e.g., CCCCCCCCCCCCC1OC1) and the acrylate is an unsaturated short-chain ester (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC), high transfection efficiency may be achieved at a moderate acrylate ratio (e.g., 0.5), challenging rule_032's view that such combinations tend toward low efficiency. This indicates that the high-efficiency synergy of unsaturated esters with epoxides may not be limited to short-chain epoxides.

When the epoxide is absent and the dioxaphospholane contains a specific unsaturated branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC), high transfection efficiency may still be achieved in combination with certain branched-ester acrylates (e.g., OC(C)CCCCCC), indicating that the range of efficient synergy for this type of complex-ester dioxaphospholane is broader than described in rule_057.

When a fluorinated epoxide is combined with a complex dioxaphospholane containing an unsaturated long chain and a branched ester structure (e.g., OCCC/C=C/CCCCC), with the acrylate absent, at a low ratio (e.g., 0.25), high transfection efficiency may be achieved, extending the applicable range of rule_039 and indicating the synergistic potential between fluorinated epoxides and this specific complex ester structure.

When a medium-short-chain epoxide (e.g., 7 carbons, CCCCCC1OC1) is combined with an ultra-long straight-chain acrylate (≥16 carbons, e.g., OCCCCCCCCCCCCCCCC) at a low ratio (0.25) and a higher backbone equivalent (3), high transfection efficiency may be achieved. This challenges the view that medium-short-chain epoxides are only efficient in synergy with short-chain esters, indicating that its high-efficiency pathway can extend to ultra-long straight-chain esters.

When a fluorinated epoxide is combined with an unsaturated short-chain-ester acrylate (e.g., OCCCC/C=C/CC) at a low ratio (0.25), high transfection efficiency may be achieved, and the backbone equivalent requirement may not be high (e.g., 2). This extends the possibility that fluorinated epoxides can achieve high efficiency in synergy with unsaturated esters, and its success conditions may be more relaxed than originally understood.

When a fluorinated epoxide is present alone (without dioxaphospholane and acrylate), high transfection efficiency may still be achieved, indicating that it has intrinsic transfection capability without requiring synergy with other components.

When the epoxide is absent and the dioxaphospholane is an ordinary long straight-chain alkyl ester (e.g., OCCCCCCCCCC), combination with a specific branched-ester acrylate (e.g., OC(CC)CCC) at a moderate ratio (0.25:0.5) may achieve high transfection efficiency, challenging the previous view that such combinations tend toward low efficiency.
